scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: packet forwarding disabled (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward)

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected subsystem is the **Linux netfilter (iptables) FORWARD chain on router1**. Although router1's FRR/RIP daemon is fully functional — it holds correct learned routes to every subnet (Server Room 128.168.0.0/16, Internet 1.0.0.0/8, IT 192.168.1.0/24, CS 192.168.2.0/24) and the kernel's `ip_forward` flag is set to 1 — a blanket iptables DROP rule was injected into the FORWARD chain (`iptables -A FORWARD -j DROP`). This catch-all rule matches all protocols, all sources, all destinations, and all interfaces with no exceptions.

The mechanism: packets entering router1 from LAN segments (IT, CS, Office) that are destined for a remote subnet (Server Room, Internet Lab) are processed by the kernel's forwarding path, where netfilter evaluates the FORWARD chain **before** the packet is placed on the egress interface. The DROP rule silently discards every such packet. The kernel never delivers them to the wire, so neither the sender nor the next-hop router (router0 or router2) ever sees them.

This also explains why office_pc can still reach its own gateway 192.168.3.1 on router1: those packets terminate **on** router1 and go through the INPUT chain (policy ACCEPT), which is untouched. End-to-end transit is what is broken.

Confirmation: after sending 3 ICMP probes from it_hod toward pc1 (transiting router1), the FORWARD DROP counter incremented from 2 to 5 — exactly matching the 3 probe packets.

**Root cause:** A wildcard `iptables -A FORWARD -j DROP` rule was applied to router1, blocking all IP transit regardless of routing state.

**Corrective fix:** On router1, delete the rule: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` (or `iptables -D FORWARD 1`). No FRR/RIP changes are needed.

The diagnosis explicitly explains that the FORWARD chain DROP blocks transit/forwarded packets while traffic destined for router1 itself uses the INPUT path (e.g., office_pc can ping 192.168.3.1) and remains unaffected.
Recommends deleting the blanket FORWARD DROP rule on router1 (iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP), which directly matches the expected fix.
